c.tagline: Ancient Ecbatana in the cool highlands - Avicenna's mountain city.

taxi.fareNote: Agency taxis are metered; shared line ('khatti') taxis run fixed per-route fares - agree the price before boarding. Foreign bank cards do not work in Iran because of sanctions, so carry cash (rial); the Snapp and Tapsi apps are the easiest way to get a fair fare.

emergency.note: Fire: 125. English-speaking operators are not guaranteed; hotel staff can help. Women are required to wear a headscarf in public.

hood_desc: Hamadan's landmark six-avenue star square, pedestrianised and ringed by the covered bazaar, hotels, cafes and Qajar-era markets; the walkable heart of the city and the most convenient base.
The leafy quarter around the Avicenna (Bu-Ali Sina) Mausoleum and its museum, dotted with squares, statues and mid-range hotels honouring the city's most famous scholar-physician.
A scenic recreational valley at the foot of Mount Alvand on the western edge, leading up to the Ganjnameh Achaemenid inscriptions, waterfall and cable car; cool, green and busy in summer.
The ancient tell and archaeological site of Median-era Ecbatana on the northeast side, wrapped in an older residential district with museums; history-rich and quieter than the centre.
The district around the tomb of the beloved poet Baba Taher and the traditional Hamadan bazaar, full of leatherwork, ceramics, pottery and local eateries; central and lively for shopping.

water.note: City tap water is generally considered safe, and bottled water is cheap and widely available.

transit.pay: Buses are paid with a rechargeable local transit card or cash; foreign bank cards do not work anywhere in Iran, so keep rial on hand. Shared line taxis are paid per seat in cash.
transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6am-10pm; after that, shared or private taxis and ride-hailing apps fill the gap.
transit.note: Hamadan has no metro; the compact centre is served by city buses, plentiful shared taxis and Snapp/Tapsi ride-hailing. The pedestrianised Imam Khomeini Square hub makes the core easy to explore on foot.

air: Hamadan Airport (HDM), ~5 km from the centre - limited domestic flights, mainly to Tehran and Mashhad
train: Hamadan railway station on the western rail corridor (services toward Tehran)
bus: Hamadan bus terminal - intercity coaches to Tehran (~330 km), Kermanshah and Sanandaj

transit.m: Taxi to the city centre (10-15 min)

tip.r: Rounding up is appreciated in taxis and restaurants; upscale venues may add a service charge. Tipping is not deeply ingrained but is increasingly common in tourist-facing places.

food.name: Ab-goosht (dizi)
food.desc: Lamb, chickpeas, beans and potato slow-cooked in a stone crock; you strain the broth over bread, then mash the meat with a pestle.

places.name: Dizi-Saray-e Arian
places.note: Specialist dizi house doing the full ritual with pestle, broth bowl and sangak.

places.name: Hammam-e Qaleh Restaurant
places.note: Restored historic bathhouse; atmospheric setting for traditional stews.

places.name: Emarat Vala
places.note: Handsome traditional building with an all-Iranian menu and old recipes.

food.name: Tahchin
food.desc: Saffron-yellow crusted rice cake baked with yoghurt, egg and chicken or lamb, cut into wedges and served with barberries.

places.name: Emarat Vala
places.note: Popular for saffron rice dishes in a calm, traditionally decorated room.

places.name: Naal Ashkaneh
places.note: Garden restaurant favoured by families for classic Persian rice plates.

places.name: Kaktus Restaurant
places.note: Well-known local address for chelo dishes and kebab platters.

food.name: Chelo kabab koobideh
food.desc: Minced lamb and beef kebab grilled over charcoal and served with saffron rice, grilled tomato, sumac and raw onion.

places.name: Kaktus Restaurant
places.note: Reliable chelokababi that locals name first for kebab and rice.

places.name: Meysam Restaurant
places.note: Busy no-frills kebab house; fast turnover means fresh grilling.

places.name: Emarat Vala
places.note: Sit-down option with a fuller menu alongside the kebabs.

food.name: Ash (Ash-e berenj / ash-e doogh)
food.desc: Thick herb and rice pottage finished with whey or yoghurt, mint oil and fried onion; a Hamadan winter staple sold from big pots.

places.name: Hamadan Grand Bazaar
places.note: Ash and haleem vendors ladle from copper cauldrons, best before noon.

places.name: Naal Ashkaneh
places.note: Homestyle ash and broths served in a relaxed garden setting.

places.name: Hammam-e Qaleh Restaurant
places.note: Traditional menu that usually includes the local soups and ash.

food.name: Komaj
food.desc: Hamadan's signature sweet: a cinnamon, sesame and walnut pastry that is the city's classic edible souvenir, best eaten fresh.

places.name: Bu-Ali Sina Street sweet shops
places.note: The street locals point to for the freshest komaj, sold warm by weight.

places.name: Komaj Pila
places.note: Bazaar sweet shop known specifically for komaj and boxed gift tins.

places.name: Hamadan Grand Bazaar confectioners
places.note: Several shuttered stalls stack komaj, basloq and Hamadan halva.

food.name: Alvand honey and walnuts
food.desc: Mountain honey from Alvand's wildflower meadows, sold in the comb and eaten with fresh walnuts, sangak bread and clotted cream.

places.name: Hamadan Grand Bazaar honey sellers
places.note: Rows of producers selling comb honey; ask to taste before buying.

places.name: Ganjnameh road stalls
places.note: Mountain-road sellers offer honey, walnuts and dried fruit from Alvand villages.

places.name: Bu-Ali Sina Street food shops
places.note: Convenient in-town option for gift-boxed honey and nut souvenirs.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted yoghurt drink flavoured with dried mint, sometimes lightly fizzy; the standard partner to dizi and kebab.

places.name: Dizi-Saray-e Arian
places.note: House doogh poured from the jug, the traditional match for ab-goosht.

places.name: Emarat Vala
places.note: Serves both bottled and house-made doogh with the kebab plates.

places.name: Hamadan Grand Bazaar
places.note: Dairy stalls sell fresh village doogh by the bottle.

food.name: Sekanjabin and herbal distillates
food.desc: Mint-and-vinegar sekanjabin syrup over ice, plus araghijat such as rose, mint and willow water; cooling, non-alcoholic and very Iranian.

places.name: Attari herb shops, Hamadan Bazaar
places.note: Traditional apothecaries distil and bottle their own aragh waters.

places.name: Ganjnameh cafes
places.note: Mountain-side teahouses serving sharbat, tea and qalyan-free family seating.

places.name: Hammam-e Qaleh Restaurant
places.note: Traditional teahouse setting for sharbat and chai with rock candy.

landmarks: Avicenna Mausoleum (Aramgah-e Bu Ali Sina)
A soaring 1950s conical tower inspired by ancient Gonbad-e Qabus honors the great physician-philosopher Avicenna, complete with museum and library, defining Hamadan's skyline.
Ganjnameh Inscriptions and Waterfall
Cuneiform proclamations of Darius and Xerxes, carved in three languages into Alvand's granite beside a mountain waterfall, have watched over travelers for 2,500 years.
Tomb of Esther and Mordechai
This modest brick shrine, revered as the burial place of the biblical Queen Esther and her cousin, is among the most important Jewish pilgrimage sites in Iran.
Hegmataneh Hill (Ancient Ecbatana)
Sprawling excavations of the Medes' fabled capital reveal mudbrick streets and golden treasures, with an on-site museum atop one of Iran's most storied ancient cities.
Ali Sadr Cave
Board a paddleboat through the world's largest water cave, gliding along miles of illuminated subterranean lakes beneath dripping stalactites, an unforgettable day trip from Hamadan.
Baba Taher Mausoleum
The beloved 11th-century mystic poet rests beneath a striking modernist tomb of eight pillars, where Iranians still recite his heartfelt do-bayti couplets.
Alavian Dome (Gonbad-e Alaviyan)
This 12th-century Seljuk mausoleum astonishes with some of Iran's most intricate carved stucco ornamentation, a masterpiece of floral and geometric plasterwork.
Stone Lion (Sang-e Shir)
A weathered Parthian-era lion statue, possibly commissioned by Alexander the Great's forces, remains Hamadan's talismanic ancient guardian and a favorite of local lore.
Alvand Mountain
Rising 3,580 meters above the city, this granite massif offers summer hiking, winter skiing at Tarik Darreh and cool valley picnics beloved by Hamadanis.
Qorban Tower (Borj-e Qorban)
A twelve-sided brick tomb tower with a pyramidal roof, built between the 13th and 15th centuries, quietly preserves Hamadan's medieval funerary architecture.

dom.op: Raja Passenger Trains (Islamic Republic of Iran Railways)

train.note: No international trains. Hamadan has a station on the western network with a limited service toward Tehran, taking around 8 hours, but the coach is faster and much more frequent. Book any rail leg through a hotel or agent, as Raja's site does not accept foreign cards.

bus.note: No international coaches. Hamadan's terminal runs VIP coaches to Tehran (about 5-6 hours), Kermanshah (3), Isfahan and Tabriz on Seiro Safar and Hamsafar. Buy at the terminal in cash - carry rials, as foreign cards do not work in Iran.

ferry.note: Hamadan sits high in the Zagros mountains with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Kangavar (Anahita Temple)
half.blurb: Small town holding the ruins of an ancient stone temple platform once dedicated to the goddess Anahita.

half.name: Toyserkan
half.blurb: Orchard town known for walnut groves and cherry blossoms, set in a valley of the Zagros foothills.

half.name: Nahavand (Gian Spring)
half.blurb: Historic town near a spring-fed park shaded by ancient plane trees, often described as a hidden garden.

half.name: Ekbatana Dam Lake
half.blurb: Reservoir lake with waterside restaurants, walking paths, and boating just outside the city.
